title: "Keeping One Reference Population: Feasibility and Diagnostics for Feature-Effect Curves"

abstract: |
  Reading a feature-effect curve presumes three things at once: a displayed
  range chosen by the analyst, one reference population held fixed across it,
  and model queries the data can support. We show that these requirements are
  jointly restrictive. A fixed reference is valid across a displayed range if
  and only if it is supported on the intersection of the pointwise valid
  context sets, so the intersection mass determines whether any such curve
  exists; pointwise admissibility does not imply simultaneous admissibility.
  We then measure the shortfall rather than assume it away. Interventional
  support coverage audits the queries an ordinary partial-dependence plot
  induces, and a support-localized envelope bounds what the unsupported share
  can do to the curve. Relaxing the requirement to a Kullback--Leibler
  projection under minimum query-validity constraints restores feasibility, and
  we quantify its price: on California Housing the intersection carries 1.3 to
  2.8 per cent of blocks, the relaxed reference retains an effective 2.6 to 5.5
  per cent, and no divergence improves that, since the effective-sample-size
  optimal projection gains at most five per cent while discarding a third of
  the contexts. A finite-sample certificate for the relaxed reference abstains
  at the sample size this application provides. A controlled stress test
  completes the picture: curves supported entirely on accepted queries are
  invariant to modifications confined to rejected ones, while the relaxed curve
  retains 39 per cent of the perturbation. Across four applications the
  intersection mass ranges from 1.3 to 73 per cent, so the contract can fail by
  a wide margin or essentially hold; which of the two occurs is a measurable
  property of the dependence structure and the displayed range rather than
  something to be assumed either way, and we give the diagnostics that decide
  it.
keywords:

## Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Partial dependence (PD) averages a fitted prediction function after replacing a
focal feature by a value $z$ [@friedman2001]. Reading the resulting curve as a
statement about the model involves an implicit contract with three clauses. The
analyst picks the displayed range. The same population of contexts is averaged
over at every point of it, since otherwise a change in the curve cannot be
attributed to the model rather than to a change in who is being averaged. And
the model is queried where data constrain it, since otherwise the curve reports
an extrapolation. Each clause is reasonable on its own.

This paper is about the fact that they are jointly restrictive. With dependent
predictors the contract usually cannot be honoured, and the obstruction is not
a defect of any estimator. A fixed reference population is valid across a
displayed range if and only if it is supported on the intersection of the
context sets that are valid at each grid point, so the mass of that
intersection decides whether a curve satisfying all three clauses exists at
all. The mass can be zero while every single grid point is individually
unproblematic: pointwise admissibility does not imply simultaneous
admissibility, and @sec-feasibility gives a construction in which it fails
completely.

Since the requirement usually cannot be met exactly, the useful question is how
far from it a given display is, and what buying feasibility costs. We therefore
proceed in three steps. First we measure the shortfall: interventional support
coverage audits the queries an ordinary PD plot induces, and a
support-localized envelope bounds what the rejected share can do to the curve.
Second we relax the requirement, replacing exact common validity with a
Kullback--Leibler projection of the context distribution under one minimum
validity constraint per grid point, and we certify that relaxation on an
independent audit split with explicit abstention. Third we price it. On
California Housing the intersection carries 1.3 to 2.8 per cent of blocks; the
relaxed reference retains an effective 2.6 to 5.5 per cent; the
effective-sample-size optimal projection improves that by at most five per cent
and only by discarding a third of the contexts outright; the certificate
abstains at the sample size the application provides; and the relaxed curve
still transmits 39 per cent of a perturbation confined to rejected queries,
where the exactly supported curves transmit none.

None of the components is new in isolation, and we do not claim otherwise. The
projection is classical [@csiszar1975; @csiszar2003; @bhattacharya1995], the
concentration tool is standard [@maurer2009empirical], and replacing the PD
averaging measure to avoid extrapolation goes back at least to @hooker2007. The
contribution is the feasibility statement that organizes them, the diagnostics
that make the shortfall measurable, and the finding that the shortfall is
structural rather than an artifact of any of these choices.

This scope is narrower than a general correction of PD. A validity rule is a
declared operational notion of query compatibility, not causal overlap or a
guarantee of model accuracy. The causal literature on positivity and on
trimming to a common-support subpopulation [@crump2009; @petersen2012] supplies
the closest analogy, and PD itself admits a back-door reading under explicit
assumptions [@zhao2021], but no such assumptions are made here. CSPD and RCPD change the reference population and
must be reported with their information distortion and effective sample size.
The empirical study therefore asks when that declared population change alters
the fitted interpretation and when it merely records a support warning.

## Setup and the feasibility of a common reference {#sec-feasibility}

Let $X=(X_j,X_{-j})$, let $P=P_{X_{-j}}$ be the original context distribution,
and let $f$ be a fitted prediction function. Ordinary PD is
$$\operatorname{PD}_j(z)=\mathbb E_P[f(z,X_{-j})].$$ {#eq-pd}
Let $s_j(z,u)$ be a prespecified validity score, with accepted queries
$\mathcal V=\{(z,u):s_j(z,u)\leq t\}$. The score, threshold, feature scaling,
and intervention range are part of the estimand. Conditional residual or
density scores ask whether $z$ is compatible with a context $u$; joint scores
also react to marginally rare contexts.

The three clauses of the reading contract can now be stated precisely. Write a
feature-effect curve in the form $T_R(z)=\mathbb E_{U\sim R}[f(z,U)]$ for a
reference distribution $R$ and a displayed grid $G$.

* **Comparability.** $R$ does not vary with $z$.
* **Support validity.** $R\{u:(z,u)\in\mathcal V\}=1$ for every $z\in G$.
* **Globality.** $G$ is the range the analyst declared, not one shrunk until
  the first two clauses happen to hold.

For a finite grid $G$, define the contexts valid everywhere and their mass by
$$
\mathcal C_j(G)=\bigcap_{z\in G}\{u:(z,u)\in\mathcal V\},
\qquad \gamma_j(G)=P\{\mathcal C_j(G)\}.
$$ {#eq-common-set}
When $\gamma_j(G)>0$, hard common-support PD is
$$
\operatorname{CSPD}_j(z;G)=
\mathbb E_P[f(z,X_{-j})\mid X_{-j}\in\mathcal C_j(G)].
$$ {#eq-cspd}
It uses one fully accepted population over the entire grid but can be unstable
when $\gamma_j(G)$ is small. Pointwise-trimmed PD instead conditions on
$\{u:(z,u)\in\mathcal V\}$ separately at every $z$; it is a moving-reference
curve and is reported as such.

The feasibility question has a one-line answer, which is what makes it useful
rather than deep.

```{=latex}
\begin{proposition}[Feasibility of a common valid reference]
\label{prop-feasibility}
```
Let $G$ be finite. A reference $R$ satisfies comparability and support validity
on $G$ if and only if $R\{\mathcal C_j(G)\}=1$. Consequently such a reference
exists if and only if $\mathcal C_j(G)\neq\emptyset$, and one that is
absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ exists if and only if
$\gamma_j(G)>0$, in which case $P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal C_j(G))$ is the unique
$P$-closest such reference in Kullback--Leibler divergence and CSPD is the
curve it induces.
```{=latex}
\end{proposition}
```

The proof is immediate: support validity at $z$ requires
$R\{\mathcal V_z\}=1$, and requiring it simultaneously for all $z\in G$
requires $R$ to put all its mass in the intersection, a finite intersection of
probability-one events. For an uncountable displayed range the same conclusion
needs additional structure on $\mathcal V$; the online supplement gives it for
interval-valued rules, where the constraint set reduces exactly to a finite
one. We state it because it
converts a vague worry about extrapolation into a measurable quantity. Whether
the contract can be honoured is decided by $\gamma_j(G)$, and $\gamma_j(G)$
is estimable from data without reference to any particular estimator or to the
fitted model.

A three-context example fixes the quantities before the machinery arrives. Let
$P$ be uniform on contexts $\{u_1,u_2,u_3\}$ and let the grid be
$G=\{z_1,z_2\}$, with the validity rule accepting
$(z_1,u_1),(z_1,u_2),(z_2,u_2)$ and $(z_2,u_3)$. Each grid point then has
support coverage $\operatorname{ISC}^P(z_1)=\operatorname{ISC}^P(z_2)=2/3$,
so a pointwise audit reports the same mild shortfall twice. The intersection,
however, is $\mathcal C=\{u_2\}$ with $\gamma=1/3$: the only curve obeying
the contract averages over a single context, and its value at $z_1$ and $z_2$
is $f(z_1,u_2)$ and $f(z_2,u_2)$, an $n=1$ summary of a population of three.
Pointwise trimming instead averages over $\{u_1,u_2\}$ at $z_1$ and
$\{u_2,u_3\}$ at $z_2$, so its two displayed values describe different
populations and their difference confounds the model response with that change.
Relaxing to a tolerance $\epsilon$ interpolates: the constraints
$w_1+w_2\geq1-\epsilon$ and $w_2+w_3\geq1-\epsilon$ force
$w_2\geq1-2\epsilon$, so at $\epsilon=0.2$ the reference must place at least
$0.6$ on the single commonly valid context and the effective sample size falls
to $2.3$ of $3$. Every mechanism the rest of the paper measures on real data is
visible here: the gap between pointwise and simultaneous validity, the
degeneracy of the exact solution, the moving population of the trimmed
alternative, and the concentration that relaxation trades against validity.

### Pointwise admissibility does not imply simultaneous admissibility

The intersection can be empty although no individual grid point looks
problematic, so $\gamma_j(G)$ cannot be inferred from pointwise diagnostics.
The construction in @fig-rotating-invalidity separates the two. There are eight
context groups and eight grid points, and a member of group $g$ is invalid only
at $z=g$. Every grid point therefore accepts seven eighths of the contexts,
which by any pointwise standard is unremarkable, while no context survives all
eight points and $\gamma_j(G)=0$ exactly. No curve satisfying comparability and
support validity exists on this grid, and no estimator can produce one.

::: {#fig-rotating-invalidity layout-ncol=2 fig-pos="H"}
![Observed mass of the eight context groups; the dashed line is $\epsilon$.](../results/s24-constraint-comparison-b.png){#fig-rotating-mass}

![Mean, minimum, and simultaneous validity under competing reference rules.](../results/s24-constraint-comparison-c.png){#fig-rotating-coverage}

Rotating invalidity separates pointwise from simultaneous admissibility: each
grid point accepts seven eighths of the contexts, yet no context is accepted
everywhere. @sec-relaxation returns to this construction to show what
relaxation recovers from it.
:::

Whether real data behave like this is not a matter of opinion, and it varies
enormously. Across the four applications of @sec-experiments the intersection
mass ranges from 1.3 per cent to 73 per cent (@tbl-gamma-applications): in one
of them the contract fails so badly that no useful curve obeys it, and in
another it essentially holds, so that hard CSPD is a perfectly serviceable
display and none of the relaxation machinery below is needed. The two are not
different in degree only.

What separates them is how strongly the focal predictor is coupled to the
context, together with how wide a range is displayed. The experiment matrix of
@sec-experiments varies both deliberately: at correlation 0.2 the intersection
carries essentially the whole population at every grid width, while at
correlation 0.8 it falls to 0.68, 0.42, and 0.10 as the displayed half-width
grows from 0.40 to 1.10. The contract is therefore a checkable property of the
dependence structure and the declared range, not a condition to be assumed
either way, and $\gamma_j(G)$ is what checks it.

  )
}
bank <- mixed_cases[[1L]]
shoppers <- mixed_cases[[2L]]
gamma_table <- rbind(

    4128L
  ),
  application_row(

 The rest of this paper is
about the case where the check fails: measure how far the ordinary curve is
from the contract (@sec-method), relax it in a controlled way
(@sec-relaxation), and report the price.

## Relation to conditional effects and balancing weights {#sec-related}

The methods in use can be read as choices about which clause of
@sec-feasibility to give up, and none of them escapes the trilemma. That
unrestricted feature replacement forces extrapolation under dependence is
established [@hooker2021]; ordinary PD gives up support validity. Conditional
PD averages under $P(X_{-j}\mid X_j=z)$ and therefore gives up comparability:
the context distribution varies with $z$, so the curve can mix the focal
response with effects of correlated features [@apley2020; @molnar2024].
Conditional-subgroup and regional methods give up globality, reporting several
local curves on interpretable partitions of the context space
[@herbinger2022; @molnar2024]. ALE accumulates local prediction
differences rather than averaging one fixed intervention distribution
[@apley2020], and its differential variant avoids constructing artificial
points altogether [@gkolemis2023]. These are valuable conditional or local descriptions, but none is
one global intervention curve over an unchanged population.

Replacing the PD averaging measure to avoid extrapolation is itself an
established idea, and @hooker2007 is its closest structural precedent. That
work replaces the product measure by a general weight $w$ and defines effects
as an $L^2$ projection under $\langle f,g\rangle_w$, explicitly because
product measures place mass where the model was never fitted. The construction
here differs in what is being built: @hooker2007 weights the joint space to
obtain a hierarchically orthogonal functional decomposition, whereas we fix a
distribution over the context variables alone, determine it by simultaneous
validity constraints across a declared grid, and report a single curve. Neither
the grid-wise intersection $\mathcal C_j(G)$ nor the query-validity constraint
system has an analogue in that decomposition.

Query plausibility and robustness also have direct precedents. Practical PDP
software uses rug marks and bivariate convex-hull restriction to discourage
interpretation away from observed data [@greenwell2017]. Manifold-restricted
interventional attributions likewise confine evaluations to a declared domain
of validity [@taufiq2023]. @yeh2021 downweight
out-of-distribution queries of individual conditional expectation curves
[@goldstein2015] when constructing an ICE-derived feature-impact measure, while @baniecki2024 bound changes in PD and ALE under data or model
perturbations. These methods respectively modify the displayed grid, an
ICE-derived summary, or the perturbation question; they do not construct one
support-qualified reference distribution used unchanged over an intervention
range. A weighted PD average is itself routine. The contribution here is the
estimand and the simultaneous query-validity rule that determine its weights.

The optimization is equally close to calibration and balancing methodology.
Survey calibration, entropy balancing, empirical-likelihood tilting, and
minimal-dispersion weights choose low-dispersion weights subject to moment or
covariate-balance restrictions [@deville1992; @kitamura1997; @hainmueller2012;
@li2018; @wang2020]. RCPD deliberately reuses that geometry. Its constraints,
however, are not covariate moments imported from a treatment group or external
target population. They are the $K$ model-query validity indicators
$h_k(U)$, and the target distribution is defined endogenously as the
KL-nearest distribution to the original contexts that makes every declared PD
query sufficiently valid. The weights depend on $P$, the validity rule,
$G$, and $\epsilon$, but not on the prediction values $f(z,U)$.

| Approach | Population represented | Distinguishing feature |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Ordinary PD | One marginal context population | No query-validity restriction |
| Conditional PD | $P(X_{-j}\mid X_j=z)$ | Population changes with $z$ |
| Conditional-subgroup PD | One population per learned subgroup | Returns several local curves |
| Geometric/OOD guards | Grid restriction or query-specific weighting | No common projected reference population |
| Entropy/calibration balancing | A sample calibrated to external moments or a causal target | Constraints encode covariate balance |
| RCPD | One KL-nearest context population for all $z\in G$ | Constraints encode simultaneous PD-query validity |

: Estimand-level comparison with the closest dependence-aware and weighting approaches. {#tbl-related-work}

## Measuring the shortfall {#sec-method}

### Interventional support coverage


For any reference distribution $R$, define
$$
\operatorname{ISC}_j^R(z)
=R\{u:(z,u)\in\mathcal V\}.
$$ {#eq-isc}

Two warnings about this name. First, the word *coverage* is used in this paper
for two unrelated quantities: the share of PD queries a declared rule accepts,
which is @eq-isc, and the frequentist coverage of the finite-sample certificate
in @sec-method below. Where confusion is possible we write *support coverage*
for the former and *tilted coverage* for the latter. Second, readers trained in
causal inference will recognize the shape of @eq-isc as a positivity or overlap
diagnostic, and the analogy is deliberate: both ask whether a contemplated
intervention has empirical backing in the contexts one wants to average over.
The analogy stops at the estimand. Positivity concerns identification of a
causal effect on an outcome under a structural model; @eq-isc concerns whether
a fitted function is being queried where data constrain it, and carries no
causal assumption.
Thus $\operatorname{ISC}_j^P(z)$ audits the exact query distribution used by
ordinary PD. If $f\in[y_-,y_+]$ and is trusted only on accepted queries, put
$m_{\mathcal V}(z)=\mathbb E_P[f(z,X_{-j})\mathbf 1\{(z,X_{-j})\in\mathcal V\}]$
and use the algebraic complement
$\operatorname{PER}_j(z)=1-\operatorname{ISC}_j^P(z)$. Ordinary PD of the
fully specified fitted function is, of course, directly computable. The
uncertainty here is a robustness question: how much could its value change if
predictions at rejected queries were replaced by another admissible extension?
For fixed $z$, define
$$
\mathcal A_z(f)=\{\widetilde f:\widetilde f(z,u)=f(z,u)
\text{ on }\mathcal V_z,\ y_-\leq\widetilde f(z,u)\leq y_+\},
\qquad \mathcal V_z=\{u:(z,u)\in\mathcal V\}.
$$ {#eq-extension-class}
The sharp range-only robustness envelope
$\{\mathbb E_P[\widetilde f(z,X_{-j})]:\widetilde f\in\mathcal A_z(f)\}$ has
endpoints
$$
\inf_{\widetilde f\in\mathcal A_z(f)}\mathbb E_P\widetilde f(z,X_{-j})
=m_{\mathcal V}(z)+y_-\operatorname{PER}_j(z),\qquad
\sup_{\widetilde f\in\mathcal A_z(f)}\mathbb E_P\widetilde f(z,X_{-j})
=m_{\mathcal V}(z)+y_+\operatorname{PER}_j(z).
$$ {#eq-range-bounds}
Sharper Lipschitz envelopes are given in the online supplement; they retain
ordinary PD as the estimand rather than replacing its reference population.

@eq-range-bounds refines a published inequality. Lemma 2 of @baniecki2024
bounds the effect of a model perturbation on partial dependence by
$\lVert f-\widetilde f\rVert_\infty$, a supremum over the whole input space
with unit multiplier. Every $\widetilde f\in\mathcal A_z(f)$ agrees with $f$
on $\mathcal V_z$ and may differ elsewhere by as much as $y_+-y_-$, so that
bound is insensitive to support and stays at its worst case however small the
rejected mass becomes. The envelope above has width
$(y_+-y_-)\operatorname{PER}_j(z)$: the supremum is localized to the rejected
region and the multiplier is the rejected query mass, so the bound vanishes as
the displayed queries become supported. Their Remark 1 tightens a constant, but it
does so for the data-perturbation bound of their Theorem 2; the refinement
here is the support localization of the model-perturbation bound.


## Relaxation and its price {#sec-relaxation}

### Relaxed common reference

For tolerance $\epsilon\in[0,1)$, let
$h_k(u)=\mathbf 1\{(z_k,u)\in\mathcal V\}$ for $G=\{z_1,\ldots,z_K\}$ and
define
$$
Q_\epsilon^*
=\arg\min_{Q\ll P}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\Vert P)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\mathbb E_Q h_k\geq1-\epsilon,\quad k=1,\ldots,K.
$$ {#eq-relaxed-projection}
The resulting curve is
$$
\operatorname{RCPD}_{j,\epsilon}(z;G)
=\mathbb E_{Q_\epsilon^*}[f(z,U)].
$$ {#eq-rcpd}

The relaxation replaces the intersection event $U\in\mathcal C_j(G)$ of
Proposition \ref{prop-feasibility} by $K$ marginal inequalities, and that
substitution is what restores feasibility: a reference can satisfy every
pointwise constraint although $\gamma_j(G)=0$. The rotating construction of
@sec-feasibility shows this at its sharpest. There no curve obeying the
contract exists, yet at $\epsilon=0.13$ the relaxed reference attains minimum
pointwise coverage
`r fmt(s24_value("Pointwise constraints", "min_coverage"), 3)` by reweighting
one context population and using it at all eight points. The constraint system
has to be pointwise for this to work: an average-only constraint achieves
nothing there, because the mean validity of $P$ is already
`r fmt(s24_value("Original P", "mean_coverage"), 3)` while its worst-point
coverage remains
`r fmt(s24_value("Average constraint", "min_coverage"), 3)`.

What is recovered is therefore not the original requirement but a graded
weakening of it, and the weakening is indexed by a quantity the analyst
declares. This also makes the construction sensitive to a representation
choice. Feasibility in the rotating example requires $\epsilon\geq1/8$, the
reciprocal of the number of groups, and in general the admissible tolerance
depends on $K$, that is, on how finely the displayed range is represented. A
grid is an analyst's choice, so a construction of this kind can be made
feasible or infeasible by refining it. The online supplement shows that for
interval-valued validity rules the constraint set reduces exactly to a finite
one and the dependence disappears; the rotating construction is deliberately
not of that form, which is what makes it a clean separating example and at the
same time the case where the representation matters. Analyses should declare
the grid before inspecting curves and report the minimum feasible tolerance, as
done throughout @sec-experiments.

```{=latex}
\begin{proposition}[Relaxed common-reference projection]
\label{prop-relaxed-reference}
```
If @eq-relaxed-projection is feasible with finite KL and admits a strictly
feasible point, its minimizer is unique and has density
$$
\frac{dQ_\epsilon^*}{dP}(u)
=\frac{\exp\{\lambda^{*\top}h(u)\}}
 {\mathbb E_P\exp\{\lambda^{*\top}h(U)\}},
\qquad \lambda^*\geq0,
$$ {#eq-exponential-tilt}
where $\lambda^*$ minimizes
$$
\log\mathbb E_P\exp\{\lambda^\top h(U)\}
-(1-\epsilon)\mathbf 1^\top\lambda.
$$ {#eq-dual}
If $P$ already satisfies the constraints, $Q_\epsilon^*=P$. When
$\gamma_j(G)>0$, $Q_\epsilon^*$ converges to
$P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal C_j(G))$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.
```{=latex}
\end{proposition}
```

This is a standard I-projection onto linear moment inequalities. It supplies a
graded validity--fidelity frontier: smaller $\epsilon$ raises validity but can
increase KL cost, maximum weight, and variance.

The divergence is a modelling choice and the weight concentration it produces
is the main cost reported below, so it deserves justification rather than
convention. With uniform base weights the Pearson divergence from $P$ equals
$n\sum_iw_i^2-1$ and the effective sample size is $1/\sum_iw_i^2$, so the
$\chi^2$ projection onto the same constraint set is exactly the
effective-sample-size-maximising feasible reference, and it is the analogue
here of minimal-dispersion balancing weights [@wang2020]. It therefore bounds
what any divergence can recover. The online supplement reports that comparison
on both the simulation designs and the California validity matrices: across
tolerances the $\chi^2$ projection improves the effective sample size by
between 0 and 5 per cent, with curve error and off-support sensitivity
unchanged to three decimal places. At the application's operating point the
effective fraction moves from 0.026 to 0.026. The concentration is therefore a
property of the query-validity constraint system and not an artifact of
choosing KL, and it cannot be optimised away by a different divergence. The
$\chi^2$ solution also assigns exactly zero weight to 36--43 per cent of
contexts, where the exponential tilt keeps every context positive; we prefer
the tilt because silently deleting more than a third of the reference
population is a larger interpretive cost than the few per cent of effective
sample size it buys. Every analysis therefore
reports minimum projected validity, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_\epsilon^*\Vert P)$,
effective sample size $1/\sum_iw_i^2$, and hard common mass. The minimum
feasible tolerance is checked before optimization. All displayed curve-shape
comparisons use common grid-mean centering,
$$g^c(z)=g(z)-|G|^{-1}\sum_{v\in G}g(v).$$ {#eq-grid-centering}


### Independent finite-sample certification

The empirical projection attains its constraints on the sample used to fit
$\lambda$; that equality is not a population guarantee. Condition on the
prediction model, validity rule, projection sample, and $M$ predeclared fitted
multiplier vectors $\lambda_c\geq0$. For an independent audit context $U$, set
$$r_c(U)=\exp\{\lambda_c^\top h(U)-\|\lambda_c\|_1\}\in(0,1].$$ {#eq-audit-tilt}
For target coverage $\tau=1-\epsilon$, candidate $c$ satisfies its population
coverage constraint at grid point $k$ exactly when
$$
\mu_{ck}=\mathbb E_P[r_c(U)\{h_k(U)-\tau\}]\geq0.
$$ {#eq-audit-moment}

```{=latex}
\begin{proposition}[Finite-sample audit certificate]
\label{prop-certified-rcpd}
```
Let $U_1,\ldots,U_m$ be i.i.d. audit contexts independent of all pre-audit
objects and put $X_{ick}=r_c(U_i)\{h_k(U_i)-\tau\}$. Let $\bar X_{ck}$ and
$S^2_{ck}$ be its sample mean and unbiased sample variance, the latter with the
$m-1$ denominator used by @maurer2009empirical, and
$B_{ck}=(1-\tau)+\tau\exp(-\lambda_{ck})$. For $m\geq2$, define
$$
L_{ck}=\bar X_{ck}
-\sqrt{\frac{2S^2_{ck}\log(2MK/\delta)}{m}}
-\frac{7B_{ck}\log(2MK/\delta)}{3(m-1)}.
$$ {#eq-audit-lcb}
Conditional on all pre-audit objects, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
every candidate satisfying $\min_kL_{ck}\geq0$ has population tilted coverage
at least $\tau$ at every grid point. Any audit-data-dependent selection among
certified candidates preserves the guarantee. If none is certified, the
procedure abstains.
```{=latex}
\end{proposition}
```

The result applies a standard empirical Bernstein bound
[@maurer2009empirical] and a union bound over candidates and grid points, in the
spirit of learn-then-test calibration [@angelopoulos2025ltt]. @eq-audit-lcb is
the lower-tail form, obtained by applying that bound, which is stated for the
upper tail, to $1-X_{ick}/B_{ck}$ and rescaling. Its
RCPD-specific step is @eq-audit-moment, which turns a self-normalized coverage
constraint into the sign of a bounded ordinary mean. We select the certified
candidate with smallest projection-sample KL cost. The guarantee is for the
frozen rule, finite grid, and predeclared family; it does not certify the
scientific adequacy of the rule, continuum coverage, or uncertainty bands for
the resulting curve. Proofs of both propositions and continuum extensions are
in the online supplement.

### Estimation protocol and scope

The prediction model and validity rule are learned on separate training and
calibration data. RCPD weights are fitted on untouched reference contexts. For
certification, those contexts are divided into projection and audit splits; a
further evaluation split is used when uncertainty for the selected curve is
reported. Calibration uses the split-conformal order statistic
$\lceil(n_{\rm cal}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, which gives marginal calibration for
the chosen score under exchangeability but does not make ISC conditionally
calibrated at fixed $z$; distribution-free conditional coverage is not
attainable in general [@barber2021], so the rule is used as a calibrated
acceptance criterion and not as a support estimator. These are predictive model-query estimands, not causal
effects.

The primary inferential target is explicitly conditional. Let
$\mathcal D_{\rm pre}$ contain the data used to fit the prediction model,
validity learner, threshold, grid, and candidate tilts. Conditional on
$\mathcal D_{\rm pre}$, the target is
$z\mapsto\mathbb E_{Q_\epsilon^*(\mathcal D_{\rm pre})}
[f_{\mathcal D_{\rm pre}}(z,U)]$. The certificate controls population
validity of this frozen, randomly learned object. It does not target a
hypothetical deterministic population validity rule. Repeating training and
calibration changes the target itself; the supplement reports this
validity-target drift separately from evaluation variation.

The five-step operational workflow, from predeclaring the grid through
certification to the diagnostics reported with the curve, is set out in the
online supplement together with its cost: forming the validity matrix takes
$O(mK)$ score evaluations and the optimization is over $K$ dual multipliers.

RCPD is useful when the scientific contrast requires one population across the
displayed range. It is not a default replacement for PD or conditional
effects. Infeasibility and failed certification force abstention. For weight
concentration there is no distribution-free universal cutoff: analyses should
predeclare a minimum effective count adequate for their desired precision and
treat violations as an unstable estimand. We additionally report the ESS
fraction, KL, and maximum weight so that severe population restriction cannot
be hidden by a smooth curve. Complete continuum reductions, active-set
asymptotics, and uncertainty diagnostics are provided in the supplement.

## Empirical evaluation {#sec-experiments}

Synthetic designs isolate mechanisms; applications establish whether they
matter. The composition design draws $U\sim N(0,1)$ and $X=U+N(0,0.45^2)$ over
21 grid points and uses two prediction surfaces that agree on every accepted
query but differ outside it, which isolates what rejected mass can do. A second
design makes the original-population effect externally known. A broader
six-model matrix varying correlation and grid width, calibration and grid
sensitivity, competing constraint semantics, and resampling diagnostics are in
the supplement, as are the exact settings of every design.

The applications are the four of @tbl-gamma-applications. California Housing
[@pace1997] is the confirmatory analysis, with median house value as response,
Longitude as focal feature, 30 prespecified splits, the central 40th--60th
percentile range, $K=21$, $\alpha=0.10$, $\epsilon\in\{0.10,0.15,0.20\}$ with
the middle value as the predeclared report, two validity learners, and
random-forest and gradient-boosting predictors. Wine Quality, Online Shoppers,
and Bank Marketing [@uci_wine_quality; @uci_online_shoppers;
@uci_bank_marketing] are held-out applications reported in the supplement; they
are included here because their intersection masses span the range over which
the reading contract goes from unusable to essentially satisfied. Bank
Marketing additionally carries a controlled stress test that modifies
predictions only at rejected queries.

## Results

### Composition and the common-reference trade-off

In the additive composition design, pointwise trimming has mean normalized
shape error
`r fmt(composition_results$normalized_shape_error[composition_results$method == "Pointwise trim" & composition_results$extension == "Upward extension"], 3)`,
whereas hard CSPD recovers the known shape to numerical precision and RCPD
reduces the error to
`r fmt(composition_results$normalized_shape_error[composition_results$method == "RCPD" & composition_results$extension == "Upward extension"], 3)`.
The two prediction functions agree on every accepted query, yet their centered
ordinary-PD curves differ by
`r fmt(composition_results$extension_sensitivity[composition_results$method == "PDP" & composition_results$extension == "Upward extension"], 3)`;
hard CSPD and pointwise trimming are invariant, and RCPD reduces the difference
to
`r fmt(composition_results$extension_sensitivity[composition_results$method == "RCPD" & composition_results$extension == "Upward extension"], 3)`
(@fig-composition). ALE performs well in this additive design and is more
robust to the off-support extension than RCPD.

Because ALE appears in every comparison that follows, we state its relationship
to these curves once rather than repeating a caveat. ALE accumulates local
conditional prediction differences from an anchor at the lower end of the
displayed range, so an ALE value is defined only up to that anchor. Endpoint
contrasts and grid-mean centering both remove the anchor constant, which is why
the comparisons here are well posed. What the centering does not remove is the
difference in estimand: an ALE contrast integrates local derivatives taken
under the conditional distribution at each point, whereas the curves studied
here are differences of averages of $f(z,\cdot)$ under one population held
fixed across $z$. ALE therefore answers a local-slope question and is not an
estimator of the fixed-reference functional, however the two are normalized. It
is retained in the figures as an informative reference point, and no claim of
dominance in either direction is made or implied by the plots.

::: {#fig-composition layout-ncol=2 fig-pos="H"}
![Centered curves against the externally known additive target.](../results/s23-composition-trap-a.png){#fig-composition-curves}

![Mean context under each reference population.](../results/s23-composition-trap-b.png){#fig-composition-context}

![Normalized shape error.](../results/s23-composition-trap-c.png){#fig-composition-error}

![Sensitivity to two prediction functions that agree on every accepted query.](../results/s23-composition-trap-d.png){#fig-composition-sensitivity}

Composition trap with an externally known additive target. Bars are twice the
Monte-Carlo standard error over 300 repetitions.
:::

A conditional-subgroup comparator on the same design is reported in the
supplement. It returns one curve per CART-induced context population rather
than a single global curve, which is a different question and not an
alternative estimator of the same quantity.


The interaction design identifies the narrower regime in which a relaxed fixed
reference helps. @tbl-external-comparison anchors every method against the
original-population effect. That target is the estimand ordinary PD is defined
to estimate, so ordinary PD attains the smallest deviation by construction and
the column is not a comparative error criterion: it measures how far each
support-qualified curve moves away from the unrestricted population, which is
precisely what support qualification is for. Read that way, the ordering among
the restricted methods is informative -- RCPD moves least, hard CSPD changes
the context mixture sharply, and pointwise trimming changes it with $z$.

The composition design in @fig-composition anchors the same methods against an
externally known additive target instead, and reverses the ordering: there
ordinary PD is the worst performer. Neither anchor is privileged. Together they
show that the ranking of these curves is a consequence of which population the
analyst declares, not a property of the estimators, which is the paper's point
rather than an inconvenience for it. We therefore make no claim that any method
dominates another on accuracy.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-external-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Externally anchored interaction comparison over 300 repetitions. The tabulated quantity is the centered sup-norm deviation from the known original-population effect, divided by its amplitude. Ordinary PD targets that effect by construction and is therefore the reference point, not a competitor; the quantity is a measure of population displacement, not of estimation error."
#| tbl-pos: H
#| results: asis
comparison_methods <- c("Ordinary PD", "RCPD", "Hard CSPD", "PTPD", "ALE")
comparison_table <- data.frame(
  Method = comparison_methods,
  `Normalized deviation` = sprintf(
    "%.3f (%.4f)",
    vapply(comparison_methods, s29_value, numeric(1),
           variable = "normalized_shape_error"),
    vapply(comparison_methods, s29_value, numeric(1),
           variable = "normalized_shape_error_mc_se")
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(comparison_table, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
             align = c("l", "r"),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

The broader simulation matrix reinforces the support diagnostic rather than a
method ranking. At correlation 0.8 and the widest grid, oracle mean ISC is
0.734 while hard common mass is only 0.076. Calibrated residual and conditional
density scores coincide in the homoskedastic Gaussian design; locally scaled
and kNN rules induce different accepted-query populations despite using the
same calibration rank. Full model-by-grid results are relegated to the
supplement.

### Finite-sample certification

The certificate audits eight predeclared projection tolerances with target
coverage 0.90 and family-wise error probability 0.10. The empirical-Bernstein
rule abstains at audit size 2,500 and certifies in
`r fmt(100 * s31_value("empirical_bernstein", 5000, "certification_rate"), 0)`\%
of 100 repetitions at size 5,000. No population violation is observed among
certified candidates on an independent deterministic 100,000-context
approximation. By contrast, the uncertified same-sample plug-in candidate
violates the population target in
`r fmt(100 * s31_value("empirical_bernstein", 5000, "naive_violation_rate"), 0)`\%
of paired repetitions. Mean selected fitting tolerance rises from
`r fmt(s31_value("empirical_bernstein", 5000, "mean_selected_epsilon"), 3)`
at 5,000 to
`r fmt(s31_value("empirical_bernstein", 20000, "mean_selected_epsilon"), 3)`
at 20,000 as the audit becomes less conservative. Hoeffding remains too
conservative to certify in this range. The complete operating-characteristic
table is in the supplement.

These operating characteristics also delimit where the certificate is usable,
and the limit is binding for the application that follows. The California
analysis holds out 4,128 evaluation contexts, which lies between the audit size
at which the empirical-Bernstein rule abstains and the size at which it
certifies, and a certified run would have to split those contexts further into
projection and audit parts. We therefore report the California curves as
projected references without a certificate, and we do not claim that the
declared certification workflow of @sec-method has been exercised on real data.
On this dataset the honest outcome of that workflow is abstention. The
certificate is a statement about what can be guaranteed at a given audit size,
and at the sample sizes typical of a single tabular application it guarantees
little; demonstrating it therefore requires either a larger dataset or a
tolerance for abstention as the reported result.

### California Housing

The two fitted models have comparable median held-out RMSE
(`r fmt(s33_value("Gradient boosting", "Conditional Gaussian density", 0.15, "median_rmse"), 3)`
for boosting and
`r fmt(s33_value("Random forest", "Conditional Gaussian density", 0.15, "median_rmse"), 3)`
for the forest), yet common-reference restriction changes their Longitude
contrasts differently. Raw endpoint contrasts below are followed in parentheses
by the contrast divided by the held-out prediction IQR.

At $\epsilon=0.15$, the forest's median ordinary-PD contrast is
`r s33_endpoint("Random forest", "Conditional Gaussian density", "pd")`.
RCPD changes it to
`r s33_endpoint("Random forest", "Conditional Gaussian density", "rcpd")`
under density validity and
`r s33_endpoint("Random forest", "Locally scaled residual", "rcpd")`
under locally scaled residual validity. The signs differ from ordinary PD in
all 30 splits for both rules. For boosting, ordinary PD is more strongly
negative (`r s33_endpoint("Gradient boosting", "Conditional Gaussian density", "pd")`),
while RCPD attenuates it to
`r s33_endpoint("Gradient boosting", "Conditional Gaussian density", "rcpd")`
and
`r s33_endpoint("Gradient boosting", "Locally scaled residual", "rcpd")`.
ALE is shown for reference under the reading set out in @sec-experiments.

::: {#fig-california-heldout layout-ncol=2}
![Forest; density validity.](../results/s33-california-longitude-application-a.png){#fig-california-forest-density}

![Forest; scaled-residual validity.](../results/s33-california-longitude-application-b.png){#fig-california-forest-scaled}

![Boosting; density validity.](../results/s33-california-longitude-application-c.png){#fig-california-boosting-density}

![Boosting; scaled-residual validity.](../results/s33-california-longitude-application-d.png){#fig-california-boosting-scaled}

Held-out repeated-split California Housing application. Endpoint contrasts compare the
ends of the central 20% Longitude interval. Points are 30 fresh splits; boxes
summarize their distributions.
:::

The population change is substantial and must temper the interpretation. At
$\epsilon=0.15$, the smallest median original-reference ISC is
`r fmt(min(s33_audit_value("Conditional Gaussian density", "min_isc_median"), s33_audit_value("Locally scaled residual", "min_isc_median")), 3)`.

The quantity Proposition \ref{prop-feasibility} identifies as decisive is
small on these data. The median hard common mass $\gamma_j(G)$ is
`r fmt(s33_value("Random forest", "Conditional Gaussian density", 0.15, "median_gamma"), 4)`
under density validity and
`r fmt(s33_value("Random forest", "Locally scaled residual", 0.15, "median_gamma"), 4)`
under the scaled-residual rule, so a curve honouring comparability and support
validity exactly would average over one to three per cent of the blocks. That
is the sense in which the reading contract fails here: it fails by a wide
margin, and it fails for both declared rules.

Median effective fractions are
`r fmt(s33_audit_value("Conditional Gaussian density", "rcpd_ess_fraction_median"), 3)`
and
`r fmt(s33_audit_value("Locally scaled residual", "rcpd_ess_fraction_median"), 3)`,
with KL costs
`r fmt(s33_audit_value("Conditional Gaussian density", "rcpd_kl_median"), 2)`
and
`r fmt(s33_audit_value("Locally scaled residual", "rcpd_kl_median"), 2)`.
The declared rule, not only the declared tolerance, drives the reported
magnitude. The two boosting attenuations above differ by roughly a factor of
two, and the spread across the 30 splits under the scaled-residual rule is
wider than the attenuation itself. The direction of the forest result is
reproducible across all 30 splits; its size is not a stable quantity but a
consequence of a modelling choice that the analyst must declare and defend.
Reporting an RCPD curve without its validity rule, tolerance, effective sample
size, and KL cost is therefore not interpretable.

Thus RCPD reveals a different, small effective subpopulation rather than a
correction toward a privileged truth. Complete balance, active-set, and
sensitivity diagnostics are in the supplement.

Two limits of this evidence should be stated. The 30 splits are drawn from one
dataset of 20,640 blocks and overlap heavily, so they quantify split-to-split
stability of the procedure and not independent replication. And no uncertainty
statement accompanies the selected curve itself: the intervals shown summarize
variation across splits, not sampling error of the displayed RCPD estimate
conditional on the learned reference. The application therefore supports
claims about reproducibility and direction, not about magnitude.

The reference-population diagnostics in @fig-california-reference make that
change concrete. Both validity rules upweight blocks with systematically
different Latitude, income, housing, and occupancy profiles; the interquartile
ranges across the 30 splits show that the shifts are reproducible rather than
an isolated split artifact. The covariance identity in @eq-rcpd-covariance
then links those fixed weight shifts to the fitted curve: RCPD differs from PD
only where the projected weights align with prediction heterogeneity. The
weights are chosen without inspecting either prediction model, yet their same
geographic/contextual shift interacts differently with forest and boosting
predictions.

$$
\operatorname{RCPD}_{j,\epsilon}(z;G)-\operatorname{PD}_j(z)
=\operatorname{Cov}_P\!\left\{
\frac{dQ_\epsilon^*}{dP}(U),f(z,U)\right\}.
$$ {#eq-rcpd-covariance}

Replacing the reference population is a distribution perturbation, so the
governing prior bound here is Theorem 2 of @baniecki2024 rather than the
model-perturbation bound discussed in @sec-method: that theorem limits the
displacement by $2B\,d_{\mathrm{TV}}$ for bounded predictions.
@eq-rcpd-covariance is exact rather than an inequality and is informative in a
different way, because it attributes the displacement to the alignment between
the projected weights and prediction heterogeneity instead of bounding it by a
worst case. The two statements are complementary: the total-variation bound
says how large the displacement can be, the covariance identity says what
produces it.

::: {#fig-california-reference layout-ncol=2}
![Standardized context-mean shifts under the projected references; points are medians and segments are interquartile ranges across splits.](../results/s33-california-reference-diagnostics-a.png){#fig-california-balance}

![Centered covariance path linking fixed population shifts to model-specific curve changes.](../results/s33-california-reference-diagnostics-b.png){#fig-california-covariance}

Who the California RCPD reference population represents at $\epsilon=0.15$.
:::

### Off-support stress test

Following the manipulation logic of @xin2025, the Bank Marketing experiment
adds a fixed logit shift only to rejected age queries. The original and modified
predictors agree on every accepted query and on
`r fmt(100 * bank_stress$observed_unchanged_fraction, 1)`\% of held-out observed
records; held-out Brier score changes from
`r fmt(bank_stress$original_brier, 3)` to
`r fmt(bank_stress$stressed_brier, 3)`, a relatively modest change compared
with the PD perturbation. Nevertheless, the centered ordinary-PD
curve changes by `r fmt(s32_distance("Ordinary PD"), 3)` in sup norm. RCPD
attenuates the change to `r fmt(s32_distance("RCPD"), 3)`, while hard CSPD and
pointwise trimming are invariant because the perturbation is zero on all their
queried pairs (@fig-bank-stress).

This comparison is unfavourable to the relaxed curve and we state it plainly.
RCPD retains
`r fmt(100 * s32_distance("RCPD") / s32_distance("Ordinary PD"), 0)`\% of the
ordinary-PD perturbation, whereas the two curves supported entirely on accepted
queries retain none of it. The same ordering appears in the composition
simulation (@fig-composition). Relaxation buys feasibility, and it pays for it
in exactly this currency: a reference that keeps mass outside the common valid
set keeps a share of whatever happens there. An analyst whose sole concern is
insensitivity to unsupported predictions should use hard CSPD or pointwise
trimming, accepting the empty common set or the moving reference that those
choices bring. RCPD is the option for the case where a fixed reference is
required and the hard common set is too small to support one.

::: {#fig-bank-stress layout="[[2,1]]" fig-pos="H"}
![Original and perturbed curves.](../results/s32-bank-offsupport-stress-a.png){#fig-bank-stress-curves}

![Centered sup-norm sensitivity.](../results/s32-bank-offsupport-stress-b.png){#fig-bank-stress-distance}

Controlled off-support perturbation on held-out Bank Marketing contexts. This
isolates a failure mode; it is not evidence that the fitted model naturally
contains the adversarial extension.
:::

## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The reading contract set out in @sec-introduction is usually not satisfiable,
and this paper's main content is the evidence for that claim together with the
diagnostics that make it checkable. Four measurements point the same way and
none depends on the others. The intersection that
Proposition \ref{prop-feasibility} shows to be necessary carries 1.3 to 2.8
per cent of California blocks. Relaxing to a projected reference leaves an
effective 2.6 to 5.5 per cent, and the effective-sample-size optimal projection
improves that by at most five per cent, so the concentration is a property of
the constraint system and not of the divergence. The finite-sample certificate
abstains at the audit size this application provides. And a perturbation
confined to rejected queries still moves the relaxed curve by 39 per cent of
its effect on ordinary PD, where the exactly supported curves do not move at
all. Pointwise diagnostics cannot anticipate any of this, because
@sec-feasibility shows that every grid point can look unremarkable while the
intersection is empty.

The practical consequence is a reporting standard rather than a new default
curve. An analyst who displays a feature-effect plot over a declared range
should report $\gamma_j(G)$ and the pointwise support coverage profile, and
should state which of the three clauses has been given up: ordinary PD gives up
support validity, pointwise trimming gives up comparability, ALE and
conditional effects give up the fixed-population intervention target, and the
relaxed reference gives up exact validity in exchange for a declared tolerance,
reporting its effective sample size and information distortion. None of these
is a corrected PD, and the choice among them is a question about the scientific
target, not about estimator quality.

Where a fixed reference is genuinely required, the relaxed projection is the
best option we know of, and its limits should be stated with it. It is
dominated on robustness by the exactly supported curves whenever those are
feasible, so it is the right choice only when they are not. Its weights depend
on the declared validity rule strongly enough to move the California
attenuation by a factor of two, which makes the rule part of the reported
estimand rather than a tuning detail. And its certificate binds only at audit
sizes larger than a single tabular application typically supplies.

Three limitations bound what we have shown. The validity rule is a declared
operational object, so every number here is conditional on it; we vary it and
report the sensitivity, but we cannot remove the dependence. The 30 California
splits come from one dataset and overlap heavily, so they establish
reproducibility of direction rather than independent replication, and no
uncertainty statement accompanies the selected curve. And the feasibility
statement is a statement about a class of curves of the form
$\mathbb E_R[f(z,U)]$ with $R$ fixed; methods that change the intervention
semantics, such as causal dependence plots or generative reconstructions, are
outside it and are not addressed by these results. Certified continuum
constraints and inference for learned validity rules remain open.

## Code and data availability

The research archive is deposited on Zenodo under
DOI [10.5281/zenodo.22904255](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22904255) and
developed at <https://github.com/mchlbckr/pdp-common-reference>. It contains
the R implementation, unit tests, fixed seeds, stored result objects,
`renv.lock`, and a `targets` pipeline that regenerates every reported table and
figure. The manuscript sources are included, so each reported number can be
traced to the target object it is computed from.

No raw data is redistributed. The archive documents, for every dataset, the
original source, licence, download command, and SHA-256 checksum needed to
reconstruct the exact inputs.
